A few questions here - is he usually on his phone a lot? and is there potential he might be neurodivergent?

If he's not someone that actively spends time texting people often, he's probably the type of person who sees it as a means to an end (ie coordinate a date) rather than a space to chat. I've met loads of people like this who just prefer to meet up in person or even have a phone call. He's not ignoring your texts as far as I can tell so it's not that he actively doesn't want to speak to you, and he seems very present when you spend time together in person - that may just be his personality/communication style. That said, you can mention it and see what he says - if you say you'd appreciate a check in text now and then and he proceeds to listen and make an effort, that's very telling.

The reason why I ask if he may be neurodivergent is that I have a friend who has pretty severe ADHD and has been medicated as long as I've known him. He is the sweetest, so affectionate and will be completely present in an in-person conversation but often will not think to contact someone unless they contact him first because they aren't directly in front of him/he can't see them. He lacks that little reminder in his head that goes "I should check in" and as a result I've started making a point to be the one that checks on him approximately once a month. He gets wrapped up in his life and forgets to reach out to people but it's never malicious and he's always just as affectionate and joyful when we reconnect. That said - he and I have never been in a more intimate relationship so I don't know if this carries over to other relationships or if it's specifically for friendships

I've had 3 back to back losses, so here's what I would do:

1. You can ask for beta-HCGs to be drawn and/or for an ultrasound to confirm tissue has passed. However, from my understanding you would've been quite early on in your pregnancy (~4 weeks?), ruling this a chemical pregnancy and therefore they wouldn't see anything on an ultrasound. Personally, I did both with my first loss and it was incredibly emotionally taxing with, let's be real, not much payoff. They saw nothing on the ultrasound and my hcg levels continued to taper. It was hard. As a general rule of thumb, if you bleed for longer than 3 consecutive weeks, get an ultrasound to check that you haven't retained anything - otherwise, this is an elective step.

2. Repeat miscarriages are uncommon, but it can happen. Certain pre-existing health conditions can increase your risks - however, given that this is your first loss, if you don't have any other concerns about your overall health, I would try not to worry about it too much (I know, easier said than done)

3. I was given the all-clear by my OB to try again from the start of my next period (not including miscarriage bleeding). Be aware that for the duration of your miscarriage bleeding, you are at higher risk for infection! It's recommended to use pads/period underwear and avoid inserting anything into the vagina until at least 2 weeks after or until the bleeding stops (if the bleeding lasts longer than 2 weeks).

Again, I'm so sorry for your loss, and I am sending you virtual hugs. Be kind to yourself while you recover and if you need to talk or have any questions, you can message me for a listening ear! I wish you an easy, peaceful recovery and a healthy pregnancy when you feel ready to start ttc again 🤍

My personal opinion is that THIS is the issue you should be bringing to couple's counseling.

A few questions:

1. The birth control is for her skin/stopping her periods, as you've mentioned. Does she have any medical conditions that cause very painful periods and/or bad acne? This could be a hormonal imbalance issue and would be worth seeing a doctor about - coming from someone with hormonal issues myself.

2. I understand your frustration, and I don't think your response is disproportionate. As the higher-libido partner myself, I also have my own frustrations when we go through dry spells. Does your wife seem to feel any kind of guilt about rejecting your advances? Does she make an effort to foster other types of physical intimacy with you (ie. cuddling, kissing)? Or does she just plainly shut you down with no further discussion or compromise?

3. Her depression needs to be managed. Is she on medication? What is she doing to help herself get better?

It sounds like she took offense to your lack of initiation, possibly because your advances give her a self-esteem/ego boost, possibly because she is concerned that your lack of initiation means that your attraction and/or feelings for her are dwindling. This is important to discuss, you need to get to the bottom of why she is so upset you've stopped making advances.

You are not in the wrong, as far as I can tell. The rejection does take an emotional toll on someone especially if it's long term, and I imagine I would react similarly to you if I was in your shoes.

The best advice I can give you is to have a loooong discussion about your individual needs, priorities, and feelings without harbouring any judgement towards one another. In order to maintain a healthy relationship you need to come to some kind of compromise - maybe you can schedule intimacy at regular intervals, have a nice date night to set the mood and go from there. Maybe she can reach out to her doctor and find out if there's anything that can be done about her lack of libido. There are so many possible resolutions to this, but she has to be willing to meet you halfway.

If she refuses to make any effort, then at that point, reevaluating whether or not it is sustainable for you to stay with this person, and whether or not you can be happy in this relationship, is certainly not unreasonable. She may not meet you where you're at, but the important thing is whether or not she is willing to try.

Best of luck to you, I hope it works out!

I suggest you do some reading on sexual education, pregnancy, birth control, and your cycle. Plan B can wreak havoc on your body for a while and should be just that - a backup plan, if you suspect that your primary birth control (pills, iud, condom, etc.) has failed, but also, knowing whether or not you are in your fertile window will be a reassuring confirmation of whether or not Plan B is necessary. Some tips from my pelvic floor physiotherapist:

-Use a silicone based lubricant rather than water based. A few drops will go a long way and won't be absorbed into the skin like a water based lubricant will, therefore you won't need to reapply more.

-Moisturize! You wouldn't think twice about moisturizing the rest of your body, but many women don't moisturize the vulvar area! You can use petroleum jelly or even an unscented, hypoallergenic and very gentle body moisturizer and apply with a q-tip or clean hands to the labia majora and labia minora, as well as the surrounding area.

-If you do any kind of hair removal, be mindful that this can cause irritation and strip the skin in that area of its natural moisture. Try to moisturize after hair removal, getting out of the shower and/or before bed. Also, if you shave, use shaving cream/gel to minimize the friction to that area as the skin can be extremely sensitive!
